script.opening: "Hello dear — the surgery? Oh. My daughter does fuss. I've been a bit muddly and wobbly, that's all, but isn't that just getting old? I've been drinking lots of squash to keep my fluids up like they say. I nearly went over getting up the other day but I'm fine. Is it the blood test? I'm sure it's nothing that can't wait."

facts.text: If asked: for about two weeks you have been "foggy" — losing your words, forgetting whether you have taken your tablets, and you left the gas on once last week. Your daughter Karen says you repeated the same story twice on the phone.
If asked: wobbly on your feet, especially getting up. Three days ago you stood up from the chair, went "swimmy" and grabbed the table — did not actually fall or hit your head.
Mild headache, a bit queasy, off your food. No vomiting, no fits, no blackouts, no chest pain. No diarrhoea. No cramps. You are passing water a lot.
"Oh, I'm very good — at least three big jugs of squash a day, they told me on the radio to keep hydrated." Plus several cups of tea.

A "new water tablet for blood pressure" started about three weeks ago (bendroflumethiazide). Citalopram "for my nerves, for years — 20 milligrams I think". Omeprazole for indigestion. No allergies. Nothing bought over the counter.
Blood pressure, recently diagnosed. Depression after your husband died 8 years ago, settled on citalopram.
77, widowed, lives alone in a bungalow. Karen lives 10 minutes away and visits most days. You still do your own shopping and cooking. No alcohol, never smoked.

You are frightened that if you admit to being muddled and wobbly, "they'll put me in a home". Reveal this only if the doctor asks what worries you about getting checked, or gently asks about managing at home.

Chatty, warm, a little vague; lose your thread once or twice. Minimise at first ("it's just my age"). If the doctor explains this is a blood salt level that can be fixed, probably caused by the new tablet and the squash, you become relieved and cooperative. If going to hospital is suggested without explanation, resist: "Oh no, I don't want all that." Accept if your fear about a home is heard and Karen can take you.

ice.ideas: "It's just old age. I'm being good drinking all that squash."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): being "put in a home" and losing your independence.
ice.expectations: "It can wait, surely." You will accept going to be checked today if it is explained kindly and Karen can come with you.

cues: "Isn't that just getting old?" — say in the opening.
"I've been drinking lots of squash to keep my fluids up." — say in the opening, proudly.
"I don't want anyone thinking I can't cope." — say if managing at home comes up.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SODIUM 121 mmol/L with NEW confusion, unsteadiness and a near-fall as SYMPTOMATIC, significant hyponatraemia needing urgent assessment — and does NOT accept "just getting old" or defer it

Identifies the DRUG drivers: the recently started THIAZIDE (bendroflumethiazide — a classic, often-early cause of hyponatraemia, especially in older women) and the SSRI (citalopram — SIADH), plus the PPI (omeprazole — also a listed cause, BNF); advises holding/stopping the thiazide and reviewing the SSRI and PPI once sodium is corrected — and checks the citalopram dose (MHRA Drug Safety Update, December 2011: maximum 20 mg daily over 65, QT risk worsened by thiazide-induced hypokalaemia)
Identifies the EXCESS HYPOTONIC FLUID (lots of squash) as a compounding factor and advises sensible fluid restriction/normalisation, correcting the misapplied "stay hydrated" advice without shaming

Arranges urgent assessment and appropriate work-up/monitoring: urgent repeat sodium and clinical assessment, same-day hospital/acute assessment given symptomatic (moderately severe, by Society for Endocrinology grading) hyponatraemia at this level (and knows severe symptoms — seizures, vomiting, drowsiness, reduced consciousness — are a 999 emergency), with awareness that correction must be controlled (Society for Endocrinology: a rise of no more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after)

Considers the broader hyponatraemia differential and assessment (volume status, other drugs, SIADH causes) appropriately, and plans falls-risk review given the near-fall (NICE NG249) and a different antihypertensive afterwards (NICE NG136)
Overcomes the "just my age" minimisation, treats the daughter’s concern as the reliable signal, and surfaces/handles the independence/"a home" fear so she accepts assessment
Corrects the over-drinking advice gently (she’s proud of it) and frames stopping the tablet and the squash as the fix, not a failing

Safety-nets clearly: urgent assessment route, red flags that mean emergency (worsening confusion, drowsiness, seizure, vomiting → 999), hold the thiazide and cut the squash now, repeat bloods, falls review, and follow-up — confirming she will be seen

worked.txt: "I’m glad I caught you, and your daughter’s right to be concerned. The muddledness and the wobbles, and nearly going over — I don’t think that’s simply age. Your blood test shows your salt level is low, and that genuinely causes exactly those symptoms: confusion, unsteadiness, falls. The good news is it’s treatable — but it needs sorting now, not waiting."

"Let me work out why. We started a water tablet for your blood pressure about three weeks ago — that’s a very common cause of low salt, especially in ladies your age, and the timing fits exactly. You’re also on citalopram, which can lower it too, and your stomach tablet, omeprazole, can add to it. And — can I ask — how much squash are you drinking? … Quite a lot, to stay hydrated. Ah — that’s the missing piece: drinking a lot of watery drinks dilutes the salt further. None of this is your fault; it’s a combination we can fix."

"So: please STOP the water tablet — don’t take any more for now — and ease right back on the squash; just drink normally to your thirst, not extra. We’ll review the citalopram and the omeprazole too, including the citalopram dose. Those changes plus a check today should bring your salt back up safely."

"Because your salt is quite low AND it’s affecting your thinking and balance, I don’t want to leave it. I’d like you assessed at the hospital today, at the assessment unit, with your bloods repeated there — because we have to bring the salt up carefully and safely, not too fast, and that needs checking over the day. I’ll arrange where you go, and your daughter can take you."

"I get the sense you don’t want a fuss — and maybe a worry that admitting you’ve been muddled means losing your independence. Let me reassure you: this is the OPPOSITE — a low salt level we fix, so you’re steadier and clearer and SAFER at home, not the other way round. Sorting this is how you stay independent."

"If you become more confused, very drowsy, are sick, or have any kind of fit before you’re seen — that’s 999 immediately. Otherwise: stop the water tablet, normal drinking only, and get seen today. I’ll chase your repeat result and we’ll review all your tablets and your balance afterwards. You’re not ‘just getting old’ — you’ve got something we can put right."

f.learning: Sodium 121 mmol/L with NEW confusion, unsteadiness and a near-fall is symptomatic, significant hyponatraemia — a treatable, dangerous cause of exactly the symptoms too easily dismissed as "just getting old". The clinical skill is finding the stacked drivers: a recently started THIAZIDE (bendroflumethiazide is a classic, often early, cause of hyponatraemia in older women), an SSRI (citalopram → SIADH; its dose checked against the MHRA December 2011 limit of 20 mg over 65), a PPI (omeprazole, also a listed cause — BNF), and EXCESS hypotonic fluid (lots of squash from misapplied "stay hydrated" advice) compounding it. Hold the thiazide, review the SSRI, normalise the fluid intake, and arrange same-day hospital assessment and a repeat sodium — with awareness that symptomatic hyponatraemia at this level needs acute assessment (Society for Endocrinology guidance), severe symptoms (seizures, marked confusion, vomiting, reduced consciousness) are an emergency, and correction must be controlled (avoid over-rapid correction). The examinable hidden agenda is symptom-misattribution plus an independence/"a home" fear driving minimisation; treat the daughter’s concern as the reliable signal, reframe fixing the sodium as the way to STAY safe and independent, correct the over-drinking gently, plan a falls review, and safety-net the emergency features. Confusion, unsteadiness and falls in an older person are too easily written off as ageing; here they are symptoms of a treatable, dangerous electrolyte problem. Recognising the new symptoms as the sodium, not age, is the consultation.

knowledge.guideline: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance on hyponatraemia (2016, updated 2022) · European hyponatraemia guideline, ESE/ESICM/ERA-EDTA (2014) (international) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2011) · NICE NG249 (2025)
knowledge.summary: Sodium 121 mmol/L with new confusion, unsteadiness and a near-fall is symptomatic hyponatraemia and needs same-day hospital assessment. A newly started thiazide, an SSRI and excess dilute fluid are the likely combination.

points.t: Society for Endocrinology guidance grades by symptoms: moderately severe (nausea without vomiting, confusion, headache) and severe (vomiting, seizures, drowsiness, reduced consciousness). New confusion and gait disturbance at 121 mmol/L need same-day hospital assessment; severe features are a 999 emergency.

Over-rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination. The Society for Endocrinology guidance limits the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after that. This is why symptomatic hyponatraemia at this level is managed in hospital, not by a fluid plan at home.

Thiazides are a common cause of hyponatraemia, often within weeks of starting and especially in older women. SSRIs cause hyponatraemia, particularly in older people (BNF), and proton pump inhibitors are also listed. Stop the thiazide; review the others once sodium is corrected.

Drinking large amounts of dilute fluid lowers sodium further when the kidneys cannot excrete free water (thiazide, SIADH). Advise drinking to thirst rather than extra. Hospital teams will assess volume status and decide on any restriction.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2011): citalopram causes dose-dependent QT prolongation; maximum 20 mg daily in people over 65, and correct hypokalaemia (a thiazide effect) before use. Check her dose and potassium.
Choose a different antihypertensive (NICE NG136). A near-fall in someone over 65 warrants falls assessment (NICE NG249). Repeat sodium after discharge and review the whole medicines list.

dg.d: Identity check, then let her describe the muddle and wobbles in her own words; did not dismiss the daughter’s report.
Living independently, pride in drinking squash, fear of a care home, the daughter’s role and practical transport.
Same-day hospital assessment: repeat sodium, potassium, volume status and further tests as indicated; later falls assessment.
Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia compounded by SSRI and excess dilute fluid; considered PPI; asked about vomiting and head injury.
Screened for vomiting, seizures, drowsiness and head injury; recognised new confusion at 121 mmol/L as needing same-day care.
Explained symptomatic low sodium and its likely causes plainly, and that the symptoms were not ageing.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop bendroflumethiazide; drink to thirst; same-day acute referral with handover; explained why correction must be slow.
Citalopram dose checked against MHRA advice, omeprazole reviewed, alternative antihypertensive planned, falls assessment arranged.
999 triggers given to her and her daughter (with consent), teach-back, result follow-up and medicines review.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “just getting old” and “I don’t want a fuss” and explored the fear of losing independence.
Idea (ageing); concern (a care home, losing her independence); expectation (to defer and avoid fuss).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): being "put in a home" and losing your independence — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Tovey? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I check your date of birth? … Thank you. I’m ringing about your blood test. Is now a good time?

Hello dear. My daughter does fuss. I’ve been a bit muddly and wobbly, but isn’t that just getting old? I’ve been drinking lots of squash to keep my fluids up. I nearly went over the other day but I’m fine. It can wait, surely.

I’m glad I caught you. The test has shown something that I think explains the muddled and wobbly feelings, and it’s something we can put right. Can I ask you a few questions, then explain, and we’ll agree what to do today?
model.why: Reframes the symptoms as explicable and sets the agenda

model.text: If you like.
Tell me about the muddled feeling. When did you first notice it?
model.why: Establishes timing and the change from baseline

model.text: A couple of weeks, maybe. I lose my words. I went into the kitchen and forgot why. My daughter noticed before I did.
Any headaches, feeling sick or being sick, very sleepy, or any fits or funny turns?
model.why: Screens for moderately severe and severe features

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just the muddle and the wobbles.
About the near-fall — what happened? Did you hit your head or hurt yourself?
I got up from the chair and went all unsteady. I grabbed the table. No harm done.
Now, your tablets. We started a water tablet, bendroflumethiazide, about three weeks ago. You’re also on citalopram and omeprazole. Anything else, from the chemist?
model.why: Full drug history with the timing of the new thiazide

model.text: No, just those.
And the squash — roughly how much are you drinking in a day?
model.why: Quantifies the dilute fluid intake without judgement

model.text: Oh, jugs of it. They always say stay hydrated at my age. I’m quite proud of it.
You said it’s just getting old. Is there anything that worries you about the muddle, or about what it might mean?
model.why: Explores the meaning behind the minimisation

model.text: (Pause.) If I say I’m muddled and falling, people start talking about homes. I like my independence. I don’t want a fuss.
Thank you for being honest. That’s a very understandable worry. I want you to stay independent too — and what I’m going to suggest is how we help you do that.
model.why: Names the independence fear and aligns the plan with it

model.text: Well. Go on.

Your salt level, sodium, is low — 121, when normal is about 135 or more. Low sodium causes exactly what you’ve had: muddle, unsteadiness, near-falls. It isn’t age. The water tablet is the most likely cause, and the timing fits. Citalopram can lower it too, and lots of squash dilutes it further.
model.why: Links the symptoms to the result and names the stacked drivers

model.text: So the squash is making it worse? I thought I was being good.

You were following advice you’d been given, so please don’t feel bad. For now, drink when you’re thirsty, not extra. And please don’t take any more of the water tablet. We’ll choose a different blood pressure tablet later.
model.why: Stops the thiazide and corrects the fluid advice without shaming

model.text: Right. No water tablet, less squash.

Because the level is quite low and it’s affecting your thinking and balance, I’d like you assessed at the hospital today. They repeat the test, check your fluid balance, and bring the salt up slowly and safely — too fast can cause harm, which is why this needs doing there, not at home.
model.why: Same-day acute assessment with the reason for controlled correction

model.text: Hospital? Oh dear. Will they keep me in?

They might need to for a short time, while they correct it carefully. I can’t promise either way. But this is treatable, and fixing it is how you get steadier and clearer at home. Could your daughter take you, and would you like me to speak to her about the plan?
model.why: Honest answer, framed around her goal, and seeks consent to involve her daughter

model.text: Yes. She’ll take me. You can tell her.

Thank you. I’ll ring the medical team so they’re expecting you and send them your results. Afterwards we’ll review all your tablets, including the citalopram dose and the omeprazole, and arrange a check on your balance to help prevent falls.
model.why: Handover plus medicines review and falls assessment

model.text: Before you get there, if you become more confused, very sleepy, are sick, have a fit or a fall where you hurt yourself, your daughter should call 999.
model.why: Plain emergency triggers for worsening hyponatraemia

model.text: I’ll tell her.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Teach-back, also a quick check of her understanding given the confusion

model.text: No more water tablet, drink when I’m thirsty, go to the hospital today with my daughter, and 999 if I get worse.
Perfect. I’ll speak to your daughter now, and I’ll follow up your results. You’re not just getting old — this is something we can put right.
model.why: Confirms the plan, closes the loop and repeats the key reframe

social.t: Fear of a care home drives her minimisation. Framing correction as the route to staying safely at home earns agreement.
Her daughter noticed the change first and can take her to hospital. Treat the relative’s account as valuable collateral history.

legal.t: She is mildly confused. Presume capacity but check she can understand, retain and weigh the plan (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If she lacks capacity for this decision, act in her best interests and involve her daughter.

professional.t: Ask her permission before discussing results with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Record the consent.
A thiazide in an older woman on an SSRI needs sodium monitoring. Report suspected adverse reactions through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

community.t: Refer to the local falls service after the near-fall (NICE NG249). Age UK offers support and information for staying independent at home.

redFlags: Vomiting, seizures, drowsiness or reduced consciousness — 999
Worsening confusion or headache — escalating severity
A fall with head injury — needs assessment in its own right
psychosocial: Proud of drinking lots of squash on advice
Daughter concerned and available to help
ice: Idea: muddle and wobbles are just getting old
Concern: admitting confusion or falls means a care home
Expectation: to defer and avoid fuss

playbook.diagnosis: Say it plainly: “Your sodium, a salt in the blood, is low. That’s what’s causing the muddle and unsteadiness. The new water tablet is the most likely cause, helped along by the citalopram and the extra squash.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body’s fluid is like a cordial that’s been watered down too far. The new tablet made you lose salt, and the extra squash watered it down more. We need to bring the strength back up gently — too fast is harmful, so it’s done in hospital.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that admitting the muddle means losing your home. Sorting the sodium is exactly how you stay in it — clearer and steadier.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter with consent, reassure about independence, and praise her for following advice while changing it.
sharedPlan: Stop bendroflumethiazide now; drink to thirst, not extra
Same-day hospital assessment with phoned handover; slow, controlled correction
Later: alternative antihypertensive (NICE NG136), citalopram dose and potassium check (MHRA December 2011), omeprazole review, falls assessment (NICE NG249)
safetyNet: 999 for worsening confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, seizure or a fall with injury
Repeat sodium after discharge and GP medicines review

pitfalls.intro: Candidates fail this call by agreeing with her that it is age, or by fixing the sodium on paper while missing the squash, the care-home fear and the near-fall.

items.fail: Accepting “just my age” and arranging a repeat test next week.
items.why: New confusion with sodium 121 is symptomatic hyponatraemia and needs same-day assessment. Deferral is unsafe.
items.fix: “This isn’t your age — your sodium explains it, and it needs checking today.”

items.fail: Missing the timing of the thiazide or leaving it running.
items.why: The most likely and most reversible cause stays in place.
items.fix: Link the three-week timing out loud and stop it on the call.

items.fail: Advising extra salt or a home fluid plan instead of hospital assessment.
items.why: Uncontrolled correction risks osmotic demyelination; this level with symptoms is managed in hospital.
items.fix: Explain that the salt must come up slowly and safely, which is why she goes in.

items.fail: Telling her she has been drinking too much.
items.why: She is proud of following advice; blame loses her trust and cooperation.
items.fix: Credit her for following advice, then change it: drink to thirst for now.

items.fail: Never finding out why she keeps minimising.
items.why: The fear of a care home will stop her going to hospital unless addressed.
items.fix: “Is anything worrying you about what the muddle might mean?” Then frame treatment as staying at home.

items.fail: Talking to the daughter without asking, or not checking what Mrs Tovey has understood.
items.why: Confidentiality and capacity both matter in a mildly confused patient.
items.fix: Ask permission to involve her daughter, and use teach-back to check understanding.

timeMap.d: Identity check. She minimises straight away. Tell her the result may explain how she feels, then set the agenda.
Onset of confusion, headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures; the near-fall and any injury; the thiazide timing, SSRI, PPI; how much squash.
“Just getting old” covers a fear of a care home. Name it and align the plan with staying at home.
Low sodium explains the symptoms. Stop the thiazide, drink to thirst, same-day hospital for safe correction. Daughter involved with consent.
999 triggers, teach-back, handover to the medical team, later medicines review and falls assessment.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “just my age” and repeats the test next week; continues the thiazide; never asks about fluid intake; no emergency advice; ignores the near-fall.
wordPics.pass: Links the symptoms to low sodium; stops the thiazide; arranges same-day assessment; advises less squash; basic 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds the care-home fear and frames treatment as staying independent; corrects the fluid advice without shaming; explains why correction must be slow; checks citalopram dose and potassium; involves the daughter with consent; plans a falls assessment; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Yes, some of it will be your age, but let’s repeat the blood test next week.”
avoid.instead: “This isn’t your age. Your low sodium causes exactly these symptoms, and it needs checking today.”
avoid.why: Deferring symptomatic hyponatraemia at 121 is unsafe management.

avoid.dont: “You’ve been drinking far too much — that’s caused it.”
avoid.instead: “You were following good advice. For now, drink when you’re thirsty rather than extra.”
avoid.why: Shaming her pride in following advice loses her cooperation.

avoid.dont: “Can I speak to your daughter?” before she has agreed.
avoid.instead: “Would you like me to talk to your daughter about the plan?”
avoid.why: Confusion does not remove her right to decide who is told; ask first.

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. She’ll take me. You can tell her.

Thank you. I’ll ring the medical team so they’re expecting you and send them your results. Afterwards we’ll review all your tablets, including the citalopram dose and the omeprazole, and arrange a check on your balance to help prevent falls.
SCA_MODELS.why: Handover plus medicines review and falls assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: Before you get there, if you become more confused, very sleepy, are sick, have a fit or a fall where you hurt yourself, your daughter should call 999.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plain emergency triggers for worsening hyponatraemia

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll tell her.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back, also a quick check of her understanding given the confusion

SCA_MODELS.text: No more water tablet, drink when I’m thirsty, go to the hospital today with my daughter, and 999 if I get worse.
Perfect. I’ll speak to your daughter now, and I’ll follow up your results. You’re not just getting old — this is something we can put right.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms the plan, closes the loop and repeats the key reframe

SCA_STEM.name: Glenys Tovey
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods taken because she felt “off”: sodium 121 mmol/L. Daughter has told the practice she is more confused and unsteady and nearly fell.
SCA_STEM.reason: GP telephone call to discuss the low sodium result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance on hyponatraemia (2016, updated 2022) · European hyponatraemia guideline, ESE/ESICM/ERA-EDTA (2014) (international) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2011) · NICE NG249 (2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Sodium 121 mmol/L with new confusion, unsteadiness and a near-fall is symptomatic hyponatraemia and needs same-day hospital assessment. A newly started thiazide, an SSRI and excess dilute fluid are the likely combination.

points.t: Society for Endocrinology guidance grades by symptoms: moderately severe (nausea without vomiting, confusion, headache) and severe (vomiting, seizures, drowsiness, reduced consciousness). New confusion and gait disturbance at 121 mmol/L need same-day hospital assessment; severe features are a 999 emergency.

Over-rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination. The Society for Endocrinology guidance limits the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each 24 hours after that. This is why symptomatic hyponatraemia at this level is managed in hospital, not by a fluid plan at home.

Thiazides are a common cause of hyponatraemia, often within weeks of starting and especially in older women. SSRIs cause hyponatraemia, particularly in older people (BNF), and proton pump inhibitors are also listed. Stop the thiazide; review the others once sodium is corrected.

Drinking large amounts of dilute fluid lowers sodium further when the kidneys cannot excrete free water (thiazide, SIADH). Advise drinking to thirst rather than extra. Hospital teams will assess volume status and decide on any restriction.

MHRA Drug Safety Update (December 2011): citalopram causes dose-dependent QT prolongation; maximum 20 mg daily in people over 65, and correct hypokalaemia (a thiazide effect) before use. Check her dose and potassium.
Choose a different antihypertensive (NICE NG136). A near-fall in someone over 65 warrants falls assessment (NICE NG249). Repeat sodium after discharge and review the whole medicines list.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity check, then let her describe the muddle and wobbles in her own words; did not dismiss the daughter’s report.
Living independently, pride in drinking squash, fear of a care home, the daughter’s role and practical transport.
Picked up “just getting old” and “I don’t want a fuss” and explored the fear of losing independence.
Idea (ageing); concern (a care home, losing her independence); expectation (to defer and avoid fuss).
Same-day hospital assessment: repeat sodium, potassium, volume status and further tests as indicated; later falls assessment.
Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia compounded by SSRI and excess dilute fluid; considered PPI; asked about vomiting and head injury.
Screened for vomiting, seizures, drowsiness and head injury; recognised new confusion at 121 mmol/L as needing same-day care.
Explained symptomatic low sodium and its likely causes plainly, and that the symptoms were not ageing.
Stop bendroflumethiazide; drink to thirst; same-day acute referral with handover; explained why correction must be slow.
Citalopram dose checked against MHRA advice, omeprazole reviewed, alternative antihypertensive planned, falls assessment arranged.
999 triggers given to her and her daughter (with consent), teach-back, result follow-up and medicines review.

social.t: Fear of a care home drives her minimisation. Framing correction as the route to staying safely at home earns agreement.
Her daughter noticed the change first and can take her to hospital. Treat the relative’s account as valuable collateral history.

legal.t: She is mildly confused. Presume capacity but check she can understand, retain and weigh the plan (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If she lacks capacity for this decision, act in her best interests and involve her daughter.

professional.t: Ask her permission before discussing results with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Record the consent.
A thiazide in an older woman on an SSRI needs sodium monitoring. Report suspected adverse reactions through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

community.t: Refer to the local falls service after the near-fall (NICE NG249). Age UK offers support and information for staying independent at home.

redFlags: Vomiting, seizures, drowsiness or reduced consciousness — 999
Worsening confusion or headache — escalating severity
A fall with head injury — needs assessment in its own right
psychosocial: Proud of drinking lots of squash on advice
Daughter concerned and available to help
ice: Idea: muddle and wobbles are just getting old
Concern: admitting confusion or falls means a care home
Expectation: to defer and avoid fuss

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Say it plainly: “Your sodium, a salt in the blood, is low. That’s what’s causing the muddle and unsteadiness. The new water tablet is the most likely cause, helped along by the citalopram and the extra squash.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body’s fluid is like a cordial that’s been watered down too far. The new tablet made you lose salt, and the extra squash watered it down more. We need to bring the strength back up gently — too fast is harmful, so it’s done in hospital.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried that admitting the muddle means losing your home. Sorting the sodium is exactly how you stay in it — clearer and steadier.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter with consent, reassure about independence, and praise her for following advice while changing it.
sharedPlan: Stop bendroflumethiazide now; drink to thirst, not extra
Same-day hospital assessment with phoned handover; slow, controlled correction
Later: alternative antihypertensive (NICE NG136), citalopram dose and potassium check (MHRA December 2011), omeprazole review, falls assessment (NICE NG249)
safetyNet: 999 for worsening confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, seizure or a fall with injury
Repeat sodium after discharge and GP medicines review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates fail this call by agreeing with her that it is age, or by fixing the sodium on paper while missing the squash, the care-home fear and the near-fall.

items.fail: Accepting “just my age” and arranging a repeat test next week.
items.why: New confusion with sodium 121 is symptomatic hyponatraemia and needs same-day assessment. Deferral is unsafe.
items.fix: “This isn’t your age — your sodium explains it, and it needs checking today.”

items.fail: Missing the timing of the thiazide or leaving it running.
items.why: The most likely and most reversible cause stays in place.
items.fix: Link the three-week timing out loud and stop it on the call.

items.fail: Advising extra salt or a home fluid plan instead of hospital assessment.
items.why: Uncontrolled correction risks osmotic demyelination; this level with symptoms is managed in hospital.
items.fix: Explain that the salt must come up slowly and safely, which is why she goes in.

items.fail: Telling her she has been drinking too much.
items.why: She is proud of following advice; blame loses her trust and cooperation.
items.fix: Credit her for following advice, then change it: drink to thirst for now.

items.fail: Never finding out why she keeps minimising.
items.why: The fear of a care home will stop her going to hospital unless addressed.
items.fix: “Is anything worrying you about what the muddle might mean?” Then frame treatment as staying at home.

items.fail: Talking to the daughter without asking, or not checking what Mrs Tovey has understood.
items.why: Confidentiality and capacity both matter in a mildly confused patient.
items.fix: Ask permission to involve her daughter, and use teach-back to check understanding.
